content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Country Office in Cuba focuses on zoonoses and infectious diseases that disproportionately affect marginalized populations living in poverty. The WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, based in Egypt, emphasizes the integration of social sciences and gender perspectives in addressing health challenges. In Ghana, the WHO Country Office prioritizes innovation and technology platforms to enhance health interventions targeting infectious diseases of poverty. Similarly, the WHO Country Office in Thailand concentrates on health systems and implementation research, while the Nigeria office addresses the intersection of environment, agriculture, and infectious diseases of poverty. In China, the WHO Country Office contributes to global health initiatives through its expertise and resources. The WHO Technical Report Series No. 971 (2012) outlines research priorities for zoonoses and marginalized infections, providing a comprehensive review of the research landscape for diseases that disproportionately affect impoverished populations. This report, developed by the Disease Reference Group on Zoonoses and Marginalized Infectious Diseases of Poverty (DRG6), identifies key research priorities to support disease control efforts. The group, funded by the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR), conducted extensive reviews of research evidence and engaged in stakeholder consultations to develop these priorities. The report addresses a wide range of neglected diseases, including zoonotic helminth, protozoan, viral, and bacterial infections, all of which are closely associated with poverty. Disease-specific research issues are detailed in individual sections, highlighting the need for new or improved drugs, diagnostic tools, and vaccines where applicable. Common priorities across diseases include enhanced surveillance systems, better integration of health, livestock, agriculture, natural resources, and wildlife sectors to combat zoonotic diseases, and accurate assessments of the burden of zoonoses. The report distinguishes between micro-level priorities, which focus on specific disease interventions, and macro-level priorities, which guide broader policy-making. These macro-level priorities include improving surveillance systems, fostering cross-sectoral collaboration, and accurately quantifying the burden of zoonotic diseases to inform effective public health strategies. The WHO Technical Report Series serves as a platform for disseminating the findings of international expert groups, providing the latest scientific and technical advice on a wide range of medical and public health topics. These expert groups, composed of individuals serving in their personal capacities, contribute their knowledge without remuneration. Their views, while independent, do not necessarily reflect the official policies of WHO. The organization’s publications aim to support national health strategies, address pressing public health concerns, and promote equitable health systems based on primary healthcare principles. By facilitating the global exchange of knowledge and expertise, WHO publications contribute to the organization’s overarching goal of achieving the highest possible level of health for all people.
